newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England seen hinting at need for tax rises. [CORRECTED 15:22 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bank of England seen hinting at need for tax rises. [CORRECTED 15:22 GMT]

text.p: The Bank of England's call on Tuesday for more interest rate rises came as no surprise to most economists, but its admission that tighter monetary policy may skew Britain's economy further was taken by some as a coded message to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.

The Bank's quarterly inflation report highlighted a policy dilemma -- higher interest rates would dampen domestic demand but would also, if they pushed the pound higher, worsen the imbalance between struggling manufacturers and buoyant retailers.

"This is a clearly coded message for the Chancellor," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel. "They are saying as explicitly as they can that if the government puts taxes up they will not raise rates too far."
Brown has said he will hold a budget within two months of the May 1 election with latest speculation centring on June 10.
The Bank conceded there was "an increasing imbalance between the growth rate of manufacturing...and of services."

But Cole, despite his reading of the Bank's message, said the odds favour a rate rise before the budget, possibly when Britain's new monetary policy committee first meets. (Corrects by removing reference to monetary meeting being held on June 5 which has yet to be decided.)
Base rates were raised last week by a quarter-point to 6.25 percent.
Since Brown has given the Bank operational independence to set interest rates and it will have five members on the new nine-strong committee, the Treasury can do little to prevent further rate rises.
The Inflation Report made clear that base rates were likely to head higher at some point.
"The central projection for inflation and the risks surrounding it suggests that...there is still likely to be a need for some further moderate tightening of policy in the months ahead," it said.

The Bank acknowledged that the pound, up about 17 percent on a trade-weighted basis since August, would help underlying inflation drop well below the government's 2.5 percent target this year as well as cramping manufacturing exports.
"But that is not an adequate response to meeting the target two years or so ahead," it said.
Brown has pledged one tax rise and one tax cut in his first budget -- levying a windfall tax on privatised utilities and cutting VAT on heating fuel to five percent from eight.
But many economists expect more. Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, agreed that the Bank was sending signals to Brown about the need for fiscal tightening.
"As long as Mr Brown delivers the four billion pounds fiscal tigthening we expect, we are happy to stick to our forecast of no further rises in interest rates," Loynes said.
"But the clear implication of this report is that, should Mr Brown fail to deliver in his budget, the Bank will push rates higher."

The advantage of tax rises is that they would rein in domestic demand, which is shooting up by about four percent a year, but would not push the pound higher and tighten the noose around manufacturers. Manufacturing output rose just 1.4 percent in the year to March.
Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, said only tax rises could prevent the newly unshackled Bank from pushing rates higher.

"Last week's base rate increase has failed to eradicate the Bank's concerns over inflation in the medium-term. Taxes will have to rise in the forthcoming mini-budget if a further near-term tightening in monetary policy is to be avoided."
Cole expects Brown to deliver a fiscal tightening and said the short sterling strip, pricing in base rates around 6.75 percent by the year-end, was not far wide of the mark.
"We look for fiscal policy to shoulder the bulk of the burden from here on," he said.
